result:
The proposed answer of 18 is wrong, because the formula $k(n,p)=\lceil n/(p-1)\rceil$ is unjustified and fails on a simple case.

**Counterexample.** Take $n=p=11$ and $P(x)=(x^{11}-x)^{11}$.

- For every integer $x$, $11 \mid x^{11}-x$, so $11^{11} \mid P(x)$. This already gives $k(11,11)\ge 11$.
- Modulo 11, $P(x)\equiv x^{121}-x^{11}$ by the Frobenius identity. So the $x^{11}$ coefficient is $-1 \pmod{11}$, which is a unit.
- Multiplying $P$ by the integer inverse of that coefficient modulo $11^{11}$ makes the $x^{11}$ coefficient congruent to 1. Setting it to exactly 1 changes only that one coefficient, by a multiple of $11^{11}$, and $11^{11}\mid 11^{11}x^{11}$ for all $x$. So divisibility by $11^{11}$ is preserved, and $k(11,11)\ge 11$.

The proposed solution says $k(11,11)=2$, which contradicts this.

**The correct value.** Write $P=\sum_j c_j\,p^{\max(k-v_p(j!),0)}(x)_j$, where $(x)_j$ is the falling factorial. This describes all integer polynomials divisible by $p^k$ at every integer. The $x^n$ coefficient can equal 1 exactly when some $j\ge n$ has $p\nmid s(j,n)$ (a Stirling number of the first kind) and $v_p(j!)\ge k$. Hence $k(n,p)$ is the maximum of $v_p(j!)$ over such $j$.

For $n=11$, $p=11$, taking $j=121$ gives $v_{11}(121!)=11+1=12$. So $k(11,11)=12$, not 2.

The sum is therefore far larger than 18, and the proposed answer is incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
